analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from charging renters application, screening, and most late fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2023 with 21 House sponsors, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit owners of federally backed rental units from charging renters application fees, tenant screening and background-check fees, and late fees (unless credited back toward rent). It would also bar landlords from using credit scores and nationwide consumer reports to screen tenants, require landlords to disclose the full monthly cost including fees, past tenant litigation, pest and maintenance problems, and ten years of rent increases before a lease is signed, and direct the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to define "junk fees" in rental housing and treat reporting unpaid junk fees to credit bureaus as an unfair debt-collection practice.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters applying to or living in rental units whose properties carry federally backed mortgages or federal housing assistance — which covers a very large share of the rental market, including most units financed through FHA loans or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. They would save the one-time and recurring fees often added on top of rent, see the true monthly cost of an apartment before signing, and avoid having junk fees dinged onto their credit reports.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits owners of covered dwelling units from charging any application fee when a household applies to rent [S2].
Prohibits charging applicants for the cost of criminal history, tenant screening, consumer report, or other background checks [S2].
Prohibits late fees unless the amount is credited toward the next month's rent [S2].

Prohibits landlords from using credit scores or nationwide consumer reports when screening potential tenants, and requires pre-lease disclosures of total monthly cost including fees, past litigation with tenants, pest and maintenance issues, and the property's rent increases over the prior ten years [S2].

Directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to define rental "junk fees" and to treat furnishing information about an unpaid junk fee to a consumer reporting agency as an unfair debt-collection practice under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and property management companies would lose application-fee, screening-fee, and late-fee revenue and would have to cover the cost of background checks themselves. The tenant screening and credit reporting industry would lose the landlord-side business of pulling credit reports and scores on applicants.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans credit scores and nationwide consumer reports as screening tools outright rather than reforming their use, which would leave landlords screening on other, possibly less predictive, criteria and could mean more restrictive income or referral requirements for applicants with thin credit files [S2].
It reaches only units with federal backing or federal assistance, so the many rentals with no federal mortgage tie would still be free to charge the same fees [S2].
Landlords would bear the direct cost of mandatory background checks, and smaller owners may pass that through in rent — the bill caps fees but does not cap rent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters, the direct savings are real: application and screening fees are a recurring tax on anyone who moves, and fees tacked onto credit reports can damage credit for years. The main honest cost is on the landlord side — absorbing background-check costs and losing late-fee income, which could feed into higher base rents — and the credit-reporting ban is a blunt instrument that solves the fee problem while removing a standard risk signal landlords rely on. The biggest design limitation is scope: it only covers federally backed housing, leaving a large slice of the rental market untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services and Veterans' Affairs committees for the rest of the Congress — never brought up for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote — and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, for himself and Rep. Jimmy Gomez [S1].
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Veterans' Affairs Committee [S4].
On August 24, 2023, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, and no further action was taken for the remainder of the Congress [S4].
Twenty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and tenant screening companies keep charging application, screening, and late fees, and reporting unpaid ones to credit bureaus, unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and screening firms keep the fees

for.name: Rep. Maxwell Frost
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a cosponsor, Rep. Jimmy Gomez, at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the 118th Congress; its sole committee action was a subcommittee referral in August 2023.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never advanced the bill.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate application fees, tenant screening fees, and most late fees — revenue that typically falls on applicants and tenants — and force owners to disclose full costs and rent history up front. Their interest in keeping these fees runs directly against renters'.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and credit reporting companies
industries.note: The bill bans landlords from pulling credit scores and nationwide consumer reports on applicants and prohibits reporting rental junk fees to credit bureaus, cutting off a steady stream of landlord-paid screening inquiries and penalty-furnishings.
